title: Spain’s election could see Europe’s far-right ‘firewall’ begin to fall apart
gist: Chatham House argues Spain's 29 November 2026 snap election will likely produce a PP-Vox coalition, making Spain the national-level test case for Europe's centre right abandoning its far-right 'firewall'. Fault lines over the EU, Mercosur, Ukraine, Morocco and Gibraltar will determine whether the coalition validates or discredits the firewall ahead of a crowded 2027 European election calendar.

insights.claim: Polls ahead of Spain's 29 November 2026 snap general election show the conservative Partido Popular (PP) under Alberto Feijóo as the largest party but short of a majority, with a PP-Vox right-wing bloc holding a combined majority in the 350-seat parliament.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A right-wing change of government in the eurozone's fourth-largest economy is the base case; position for policy shifts on trade, migration and EU alignment.
insights.locator: Spain votes on Sunday 29 November

insights.claim: Convergent Opinion's MRP poll as of 22 November 2026 put PP and Vox on a combined 186 seats, 10 above the 176 needed for a majority in Spain's parliament.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A 10-seat cushion is meaningful but not insurmountable; watch turnout as the swing variable.
insights.locator: As of 22 November, Convergent Opinion’s MRP poll

insights.claim: Spain bans publishing polls in the final week before an election, precisely when voters typically decide, which leaves observers blind in the final stretch and may help the left as voters weigh tactical votes against the right.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect elevated late-surprise risk versus final published polls; don't over-anchor on pre-blackout numbers.
insights.locator: It is illegal in Spain to publish polls

insights.claim: Pedro Sánchez's only path to a left-wing victory is extraordinarily high mobilization; he is targeting 75% turnout, and despite Socialist campaign gains the bloc gap may be too wide to close otherwise.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Turnout near or above 75% is the key tail signal for an upset left-bloc result.
insights.quote: the only route to victory for the left is high mobilization
insights.locator: Sánchez has been clear

insights.claim: On current polling Vox would win 55-69 seats, close to a third of the right-wing bloc, enough to claim ministries and shape policy rather than merely lend votes from outside government — though Vox might instead choose to pressure a minority Feijóo government.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Vox holding ministries (vs. confidence-and-supply) materially raises policy-volatility risk for Spain.
insights.locator: A PP-Vox coalition government seems the most likely outcome

insights.claim: A PP-Vox national coalition would mark the first time the far right has governed in Spain since it became a democracy and would give Vox a say in Spanish foreign policy for the first time; until now the two have only governed together regionally and locally.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Historic precedent: markets have no national track record for a Vox-influenced Spanish government.
insights.locator: Until now, the PP and Vox have governed together

themes.theme: Spain as Europe's firewall test case

insights.claim: If Vox enters government, Spain becomes the test case for what happens when Europe's centre right drops its barrier to the far right at the national level (the German 'firewall'), with outsized weight because Spain is the eurozone's fourth-largest economy and has been the most outspoken progressive government among large EU states.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The Spanish outcome will be read across Europe as precedent for centre-right/far-right coalitions in France, Germany and beyond.
insights.quote: Spain will become the test case for what happens when Europe’s centre right drops its barrier to the far right
insights.locator: If Vox is brought into government, Spain will become the test case

insights.claim: Finland, Sweden and the Netherlands have already brought the far right into government or formal support arrangements, but Spain would be the largest and most symbolically significant case.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Far-right participation in European governments is becoming normalized; Spain extends it to a large eurozone economy.
insights.locator: Elsewhere in Europe, Finland, Sweden and the Netherlands

insights.claim: If a PP-Vox government holds together and keeps Spain close to the European mainstream it will be cited as proof the firewall was never needed; if it splits over Ukraine, Morocco or Brussels it will strengthen the case for keeping the firewall.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Coalition stability in Spain is a leading indicator for whether Germany's CDU and France's Les Républicains abandon their firewalls.
insights.quote: If a PP-Vox government holds together and keeps Spain close to the European mainstream, it will be cited as proof that the firewall was never needed.
insights.locator: Given an increasingly fragmented electorate

insights.claim: Given increasingly fragmented electorates, centre-right parties across Europe may need the far right to govern, as Feijóo likely will in Spain.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Structural fragmentation makes centre-right/far-right coalitions more likely across EU, raising the policy variance of European governments.
insights.locator: Given an increasingly fragmented electorate

themes.theme: PP-Vox fault lines: EU, trade, Ukraine

insights.claim: The deepest PP-Vox divide is over Europe itself: PP belongs to the European People's Party that leads EU institutions, while Vox in 2024 left the ECR to join the far more Eurosceptic Patriots for Europe founded by Viktor Orbán.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect friction on EU-level votes and Spain's posture in Brussels under a coalition.
insights.locator: Divided over Europe

insights.claim: Vox calls the EU-Mercosur trade agreement a 'betrayal' of Spanish farmers and attacks the PP for backing it, so a Feijóo-led coalition would face pressure over defending the deal in Brussels.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Risk to EU-Mercosur ratification/implementation politics; relevant for EU agriculture and South American export exposure.
insights.locator: On trade, Vox calls the EU-Mercosur trade agreement

insights.claim: Feijóo's PP supports Ukraine in line with the European centre right, but Vox's Abascal sided with Trump against Zelenskyy in 2025, has blamed Europe for financing the war, and Vox has repeatedly abstained on European Parliament resolutions.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A Vox-influenced Spain could weaken EU unanimity on Ukraine support; watch Spanish positions on Ukraine funding.
insights.locator: On Ukraine, Feijóo’s PP supports Kyiv

insights.claim: Vox's manifesto makes 'remigration' (a term borrowed from Germany's AfD) central and vows to militarize the border, yet Spain cannot easily control migration without Morocco's cooperation, setting up friction with Rabat.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A PP-Vox government raises Spain-Morocco diplomatic risk, with knock-on effects on migration flows and bilateral trade.
insights.locator: Vox’s manifesto makes ‘remigration’ a central promise

insights.claim: Feijóo, who had pledged to make Morocco his first foreign visit, has hardened his tone since the summer 2026 Ceuta border crisis, calling it an 'invasion' in a televised debate and taking a far more hostile line towards Rabat than Sánchez.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Even PP alone signals a harder Morocco stance; Spain-Morocco relations likely deteriorate under a right-wing government.
insights.locator: The PP’s Feijóo had pledged to make Morocco his first foreign visit

insights.claim: A PP-Vox government would inherit the UK-EU Gibraltar treaty, provisionally applied since 15 July 2026, which Vox calls 'illegal, illegitimate and unjust' and pledges to overturn to recover sovereignty, forcing Feijóo to choose between a dispute with London and Brussels or with his coalition partner.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Gibraltar treaty reopening risk is a new UK-EU friction point to watch.
insights.quote: ‘recover Spanish sovereignty over the Rock of Gibraltar.’
insights.locator: On Gibraltar, a PP-Vox government would inherit

insights.claim: Any future UK application to rejoin the EU would need unanimous member-state approval including Spain, and far-right gains across Europe in the next 12 months could complicate such negotiations.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: UK rejoin scenarios face a rising veto risk from far-right-influenced member governments.
insights.locator: For British EU ‘rejoiners’

insights.claim: Sánchez has made opposition to Trump central to his politics and framed the election internationally, buoyed by Lula's Brazilian election win, Democrats' big US midterm gains and Orbán losing power in Hungary in April 2026.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Spain's vote is being read as part of a transnational left-vs-populist-right contest, amplifying its signal value.
insights.quote: Sánchez has told voters that the world is watching Spain
insights.locator: Part of a wider contest

insights.claim: International right-wing figures have intervened against Sánchez: Javier Milei called him an 'unpresentable dictator' at a Madrid rally backed by messages from Meloni, Le Pen and Orbán, and Elon Musk called him 'a tyrant and a traitor' over Spain's plan to ban social media for under-16s.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Spain's under-16 social media ban puts it in direct conflict with platform owners like Musk — a tech regulation flashpoint.
insights.locator: On the other side, Argentina’s President Javier Milei

insights.claim: Spain's vote sets the tone for a crowded 2027 European electoral year: France's presidential election in April 2027 with Le Pen's Rassemblement National leading polls, plus parliamentary elections in Finland, Estonia and Greece and votes in Poland and Italy by year-end.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: European political risk calendar for 2027 is heavy; France April 2027 is the key event for OAT spreads and EU cohesion.
insights.locator: Spain’s election will therefore be important in setting the tone

themes.theme: Firewall strain and a divided left

insights.claim: Germany's CDU firewall is under more strain than ever after the far-right AfD won 44% in Saxony-Anhalt in September 2026.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: German political risk is rising; any CDU-AfD cooperation would be a major European regime shift.
insights.locator: In Germany, the far-right AfD won 44 per cent

insights.claim: In France, Les Républicains have ruled out a 2027 pact with the Rassemblement National, but the mayor of Nice's call to work with Le Pen's camp shows cracks in that line.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch for centre-right defections in France as a precursor to a Le Pen-led governing majority.
insights.locator: In France, Les Républicains have ruled out a pact

insights.claim: A divided left is a central factor in far-right victories: in Spain, Podemos and Frente Amplio failed to agree a joint list, Podemos polls at 1-2% so most of its vote will be wasted, and its attacks on Sánchez could depress left-wing turnout.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Left fragmentation mechanically boosts right-bloc seat share under Spain's electoral system.
insights.quote: A divided left is a central factor in the potential victories of the far right.
insights.locator: A divided left is a central factor

insights.claim: Left fragmentation is a Europe-wide pattern: UK Labour lost ground to the Greens in May's local elections, and in Germany a YouGov poll has the SPD at 15%, level with the Greens, with Die Linke at 10%.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Centre-left erosion across UK and Germany increases odds of centre-right reliance on the far right.
insights.locator: The pattern is not dissimilar elsewhere
